lines.t: Do you work harder when someone is watching?
People change their behavior when they know they're being observed.
In the 1920s, researchers studied workers at the Hawthorne Works factory near Chicago.
Brighter lights? Output went up. Dimmer lights? Output still went up.
The story became: workers responded to the attention, not the lights.
Henry Landsberger named it the Hawthorne effect in 1958.
It can skew studies, surveys, and performance reviews.
But a 2011 re-analysis of the lighting data found the famous pattern wasn't really there.
The effect exists, but it's usually smaller than the legend.
Takeaway: watching people can change what you see.
